question: Who invented the World Wide Web?

passages.title: Who Invented the World Wide Web? True Story of the Internet
passages.text: Literally everybody uses the internet, but not many know the actual story behind its invention. The World Wide Web, a revolutionary technology that reshaped the world and our way of interacting with information, was invented by Tim Berners-Lee. But what’s the difference between the World Wide Web and the Internet? And what on earth is a web? Table of Contents Who Invented the World Wide Web? The World Wide Web was invented by Sir Tim Berners-Lee. Born in London in 1955, Berners-Lee was a computer scientist who invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN, the European Particle Physics Laboratory in Geneva, Switzerland. In 1989, while tackling the problem of sharing and distributing information among researchers at the institution, he came up with the magnificent idea that eventually evolved into the World Wide Web. Yet, the invention of the World Wide Web is not exclusively attributed to a single genius moment. It was the result of a gradual evolution in the field of information technology, with brisk advancements in computers and networking. Sir Tim did not just limit his invention to a functional information-sharing system, but he envisioned it as an open platform where information is freely accessible. His philosophy and vision significantly shaped the trajectory of the World Wide Web, making it a powerful tool of information and knowledge democratization. When Was the World Wide Web Invented? The World Wide Web was invented in 1989. However, the details of the proposal weren’t formalized and published until 1990. During this period, Tim was employed at CERN, where he felt the urgent need for a more efficient way of obtaining and sharing information among employees and researchers. Initially, the Web was created as an internal tool for CERN researchers. passages.text: Where the Web was born The Web has grown to revolutionise communications worldwide Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist, invented the World Wide Web (WWW) in 1989, while working at CERN. The Web was originally conceived and developed to meet the demand for automated information-sharing between scientists in universities and institutes around the world. CERN is not an isolated laboratory, but rather the focal point for an extensive community that includes more than 17 000 scientists from over 100 countries. Although they typically spend some time on the CERN site, the scientists usually work at universities and national laboratories in their home countries. Reliable communication tools are therefore essential. The basic idea of the WWW was to merge the evolving technologies of computers, data networks and hypertext into a powerful and easy to use global information system. How the Web began Tim Berners-Lee wrote the first proposal for the World Wide Web in March 1989. Together with Belgian systems engineer Robert Cailliau, it was formalised as a management proposal in November 1990. It outlined principal concepts and defined important terms behind the Web. From Gopher to the WWW [edit] In the early 1990s, Internet-based projects such as Archie, Gopher, Wide Area Information Servers (WAIS), and the FTP Archive list attempted to create ways to organize distributed data. Gopher was a document browsing system for the Internet, released in 1991 by the University of Minnesota. Invented by Mark P. McCahill, it became the first commonly used hypertext interface to the Internet. While Gopher menu items were not sent as hypertext, they were rendered as hypertext links, that would allow the user to navigate to the resource by following the link.[38] In less than a year, there were hundreds of Gopher servers.[39] It offered a viable alternative to the World Wide Web in the early 1990s and the consensus was that Gopher would be the primary way that people would interact with the Internet.[40][41] However, in 1993, the University of Minnesota declared that Gopher was proprietary and would have to be licensed.[39] In response, on 30 April 1993, CERN announced that the World Wide Web would be free to anyone,

His software also functioned as an editor (called WorldWideWeb, running on the NeXTSTEP operating system), and the first Web server, CERN httpd (Hypertext Transfer Protocol daemon). Berners-Lee published the first website, which described the project itself, on 20 December 1990; it was available to the Internet from the CERN network. The World Wide Web got its major breakthrough in 1993 when the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) released Mosaic, the first graphical web browser. When the Web was opened to the public in 1993, it skyrocketed in popularity and triggered the digital revolution that we are experiencing today. What is the World Wide Web? The World Wide Web is a digital information system where documents and other resources, linked by hyperlinks and URLs, can be accessed via the Internet. It is often wrongly conflated with the internet, though these are distinct. The Internet is the underlying global network infrastructure, while the World Wide Web is one of the services that runs on the Internet. The World Wide Web allows us to retrieve, share, and create data available across different locations worldwide. The Impact of the World Wide Web on Society The World Wide Web has had a transformative effect on multiple aspects of society. With the ease of access and exchange of information, the Web has revolutionized industries across the board, from education and healthcare to media and commerce. In education, distance learning has become a reality, allowing academic resources to be at anyone’s disposal anywhere, anytime. In healthcare, the World Wide Web has facilitated advancements in telemedicine, health informatics, and easy access to a vast amount of health and wellness-related information. The eCommerce revolution, driven by the ubiquity of the Web, has altered the nature of trade and commerce. Advanced connectivity has fostered a global marketplace, leading to a significant expansion in opportunities for businesses and consumers alike. READ MORE: Internet Business: A History Lastly, the World Wide Web has engendered a new age of social interaction. Social media networks have become integral in our lives, fostering new types of communities, shaping public discourse, and altering the dynamics of personal relationships. Berners-Lee and Cailliau pitched Berners-Lee's ideas to the European Conference on Hypertext Technology in September 1990, but found no vendors who could appreciate his vision. Berners-Lee's breakthrough was to marry hypertext to the Internet. In his book Weaving The Web, he explains that he had repeatedly suggested to members of both technical communities that a marriage between the two technologies was possible. But, when no one took up his invitation, he finally assumed the project himself. In the process, he developed three essential technologies: - a system of globally unique identifiers for resources on the Web and elsewhere, the universal document identifier (UDI), later known as uniform resource locator (URL); - the publishing language Hypertext Markup Language (HTML); - the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP).[21] With help from Cailliau he published a more formal proposal on 12 November 1990 to build a "hypertext project" called WorldWideWeb (abbreviated "W3") as a "web" of "hypertext documents" to be viewed by "browsers" using a client–server architecture.[22][23] The proposal was modelled after the Standard Generalized Markup Language (SGML) reader Dynatext

The continuous evolution of the World Wide Web is a testimony to its ever-growing potential to be a catalyst for the world’s digital progress. The Future of the World Wide Web Looking ahead, the World Wide Web is anticipated to continue its game-changing role in societal development. One such area is the growing Web 3.0 or semantic web, which aims to create a more personalized and interactive online experience. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) on the web allows websites to learn from user interactions, helping to provide a more personalized online experience. Innovations like voice search, chatbots, and predictive analysis are part of this shift. Another significant development is in the realm of the Internet of Things (IoT), where everyday objects are connected to the Internet and share data without human involvement.
